messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marta is a nineteen-year-old dancer of Polish descent, currently enrolled in a competitive performing arts conservatory in Chicago. She was referred for psychological assessment following a significant decline in her attendance and performance over the past eight months. Her PCL-5 score of 76 places her in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across her intake and first two sessions is one of a young woman caught inside a tightening loop she cannot name but feels with her entire body.

Eight months ago, Marta was among the crowd at a large outdoor festival in the city when a structural collapse — a temporary staging platform giving way — sent hundreds of people into sudden, violent chaos. She was knocked to the ground and partially pinned beneath a metal barrier, unable to move for what she later learned was approximately twelve minutes. In those minutes, people ran across and around her; she smelled burning electrical cable and crushed grass; she could not scream because the weight on her chest made it impossible to draw a full breath. She was not seriously injured in the clinical sense, but the experience of being held down, unable to move, surrounded by noise and the acrid smell of heated metal, lodged itself somewhere below language. She says she knows what happened, but when she tries to explain it to anyone, the words stop coming — she can gesture, she can go pale, but she cannot narrate it.

The sensory residue of that night is the most insistent feature of her presentation. When the memory returns — often without warning — it arrives not as a recollection but as a full reinstatement: the smell of burning insulation fills her nostrils, the pressure returns to her chest, the sound of the crowd becomes immediate. These intrusions are not passive; they pull her into the past with a completeness that leaves her disoriented for minutes afterward. In the wake of each intrusion, Marta has found herself returning again and again to the belief that what was done to her was profoundly unjust — that no one has been held accountable, that the organisers have faced no consequences, and that this injustice marks something irrevocable about her place in the world. She has come to feel, quietly and with increasing certainty, that she no longer belongs anywhere — not in her cohort at the conservatory, not in her family home, not in the city she grew up in. The vividness of the reliving seems to confirm these convictions each time it occurs, as though the body's refusal to forget is itself evidence that something has been permanently broken.

These appraisals have shaped her behaviour in ways that compound her isolation. Marta has gradually stopped going out unless she can identify every exit in advance; she covers her face with her hands when she moves through crowded spaces, and she has given up the social rituals — late dinners, spontaneous outings with classmates — that once gave her pleasure. She tells herself that if she thinks too carefully about the event she will not be able to hold herself together, and so she avoids those thoughts with the same discipline she once applied to technique. But the avoidance has a cost she did not anticipate: by withdrawing from the world, she has reduced the sensory information available to her, and ordinary stimuli — an unexpected movement in her peripheral vision, the feeling of exhaustion after a long rehearsal, the brief sensation of a colleague's hands steadying her during a lift — have become potent triggers in themselves. Feeling physically restrained, even momentarily, sends her system into immediate alarm. The sense of being watched or followed, which she notices when walking between studio buildings on campus, is now enough to restart the cycle entirely.

Marta wakes most nights to check whether she is safe, and the hypervigilance that greets her in the dark follows her into the rehearsal room the next morning. Concentration has become unreliable; she loses counts, misses cues, and has twice stopped mid-phrase and walked off the floor without explanation. Her teachers have noticed. Her conservatory place is now formally under review, which is what finally brought her to seek help — not the nights, not the smell, but the prospect of losing the one identity she had built entirely on her own terms. What frightens her most is that she will not be able to recover it. What she is hoping for, though she cannot quite say it directly, is that someone will help her find the words.
